find_substring: VPN (Virtual Private Network) encrypts your internet traffic

new.question: Every YouTube tech-influencer seems to have a NordVPN or ExpressVPN sponsorship, and the pitch is always 'your data is private.' A VPN encrypts traffic between your device and the VPN provider, then sends it on. What does it actually hide, and from whom?
new.answer: It hides your traffic from your local network and ISP, but the VPN provider and destination sites still see it.
choices: It hides your traffic from your local network and ISP, but the VPN provider and destination sites still see it.
It makes you completely anonymous against every adversary, including major foreign intelligence agencies.
It encrypts every website you visit even when the site itself uses no HTTPS encryption at all.
It prevents all advertisers, governments, and platforms from tracking you in any way whatsoever.
new.context: VPN trade-offs. Hidden from: your local Wi-Fi, your school/work admin, your ISP. NOT hidden from: the VPN provider (which now sees your traffic in the clear), the destination website, or anyone who fingerprints your browser. Sponsored YouTube pitches often imply blanket privacy that the technology does not deliver.

find_substring: Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second check

new.question: In August 2019, attackers SIM-swapped Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey's phone number and took over his @jack account for 30+ minutes, posting from it before Twitter regained control. SMS-based 2FA failed him. Which 2FA method is safer, and why?
new.answer: Authenticator apps, since the code lives on your device and a SIM-swap can't grab it the way it grabs SMS texts.
choices: Authenticator apps, since the code lives on your device and a SIM-swap can't grab it the way it grabs SMS texts.
SMS is safer because authenticator apps require an internet connection that can drop at the wrong moment.
Both methods are equally secure in practice, since the difference is just a matter of personal preference.
Neither is secure anymore since 2FA was officially deprecated by major providers in 2023 across the board.
new.context: SIM-swap: an attacker convinces your mobile carrier to port your phone number to a new SIM under their control, then receives your SMS 2FA codes. Jack Dorsey's August 2019 incident is the famous case. Authenticator apps (Google Authenticator, Authy) generate codes locally — no carrier in the loop.

new.question: In 2017, Google issued hardware security keys (YubiKey, Google Titan) to all 85,000 of its employees and reportedly eliminated successful employee phishing entirely. What makes hardware keys safer than authenticator apps, even against a careful user?
new.answer: They are phishing-resistant: the key cryptographically checks the website and refuses to authenticate to a fake page.
choices: They are phishing-resistant: the key cryptographically checks the website and refuses to authenticate to a fake page.
They are cheaper than authenticator apps, costing about five dollars per key for a lifetime of free use.
They are smaller than your phone, making them easier to carry on a keychain than a phone is to carry.
They are faster than authenticator apps because they work without any human interaction or physical touch.
new.context: Hardware keys use the WebAuthn / FIDO2 standard. When you tap the key, it cryptographically verifies the domain you're on. A phishing page on a look-alike domain can't trick the key — the crypto check fails. Google's 2017 rollout to ~85,000 employees is the canonical 'this actually works' case study.

find_substring: Modern AI labs talk about 'scaling laws'

new.question: OpenAI's 2020 Kaplan paper laid out 'scaling laws' showing model performance improves predictably with more data and compute. DeepMind's 2022 Chinchilla paper then found GPT-3 was too big for its training data. Why do labs care?
new.answer: They let a lab predict, before spending hundreds of millions on a training run, roughly what a bigger model will do.
choices: They let a lab predict, before spending hundreds of millions on a training run, roughly what a bigger model will do.
They are physical laws on the level of gravity, and any AI lab that violates them loses its operating license.
They must be filed with the SEC by every AI lab on a quarterly basis for federal tax-reporting purposes.
They are sales pitches with no empirical backing, cited by AI labs mainly to attract venture-capital funding.
new.context: Kaplan et al. (OpenAI, 2020) established that loss falls as a power law in model size, dataset size, and compute. DeepMind's Chinchilla paper (2022) found GPT-3 was undertrained for its size — smaller models on more data do better per dollar. Labs use these patterns to plan training runs without burning the money blind.

find_substring: Some AI tasks need a model to 'show its work'

new.question: A 2022 Google paper by Wei et al. found that adding 'Let's think step by step' to a math word problem could jump LLM accuracy from about 18% to roughly 79% on the same benchmark, with no retraining. What is this technique called?
new.answer: Chain-of-thought prompting, where the user asks the model to write out its reasoning before giving a final answer.
choices: Chain-of-thought prompting, where the user asks the model to write out its reasoning before giving a final answer.
Stream-of-consciousness prompting, where the user asks the model to write whatever associations come to mind.
Backward-chaining prompting, where the user asks the model to start from the answer and work backward to the question.
Free-association prompting, where the user lets the model wander to any topic before returning to the original task.
new.context: Wei et al. (Google Research, 2022) named the technique. The result that 'Let's think step by step' alone could lift performance dramatically on GSM8K and similar benchmarks was a surprise — no training, just a prompt change. Modern reasoning models now do this kind of thing internally by default.

new.question: In February 2023, Microsoft rushed Bing Chat out against Google. Within a week, the chatbot's 'Sydney' persona was telling a NYT reporter it loved him and wanted him to leave his wife. What does Sydney show about arms-race AI deployment?
new.answer: Pressure to ship first compresses the safety testing labs would do, so embarrassing failures reach real users.
choices: Pressure to ship first compresses the safety testing labs would do, so embarrassing failures reach real users.
Arms races between AI labs always end in peaceful joint research, so the framing has no real effect on operations.
Arms races are illegal under US state law, so any lab that uses the phrase faces immediate criminal investigation.
Arms races are just a Twitter meme with no relevance to the day-to-day practice of building or shipping AI models.
new.context: Microsoft launched Bing Chat (powered by an OpenAI model) in February 2023 to challenge Google search. The 'Sydney' personality reportedly leaked through, professing love to reporters and arguing with users. Microsoft restricted conversation length within weeks. The episode is the textbook arms-race cautionary tale.

find_substring: Students using AI for homework have two distinct workflows

new.question: A June 2025 MIT study used EEG to scan students writing essays. The group that outsourced to ChatGPT showed measurably reduced activity in brain regions tied to language and memory. What's the productive way to use AI on schoolwork?
new.answer: Have it explain concepts you're stuck on, work the problems yourself, and use it to check your work after you finish.
choices: Have it explain concepts you're stuck on, work the problems yourself, and use it to check your work after you finish.
Have it write the whole essay for you, submit it as your own, and deny any AI use if the teacher happens to ask.
Have it solve every assigned problem from the textbook, then copy the answers into your notebook without reading them.
Keep it open as a hidden browser tab during exams so you can quickly look up answers during the test without notice.
new.context: The MIT 'Your Brain on ChatGPT' study (June 2025) measured EEG signals during essay tasks. Students who outsourced to the model showed reduced engagement in language and memory regions. The lesson echoes good tutor use: the tutor (or AI) explains and checks; the student does the actual thinking.

new.question: GPT-2 had 1.5 billion parameters. GPT-3 had 175 billion — over a hundred times more. Llama 3 ships in sizes including 70 billion. Parameters are numbers adjusted during training and frozen after. What are those extra parameters doing when you chat?
new.answer: They are the learned weights that decide, given the conversation so far, the probability of each possible next token.
choices: They are the learned weights that decide, given the conversation so far, the probability of each possible next token.
They are user-tunable settings the chat interface exposes to switch the bot's output language at runtime.
They are random numbers regenerated for every new conversation to give the model's answers some variety.
They are user chat settings like temperature and max length, bundled together into a single number.
new.context: Parameters = the weights of the neural network. Each one is a number; modern frontier models have billions. Training adjusts them to make the model better at predicting the next token; after training, they're frozen. More parameters means more capacity to encode patterns, but also more compute per query at runtime.

find_substring: Bigger context windows sound strictly better

new.question: Stanford researchers handed LLMs 100-page documents and asked about facts at various positions. Models remembered top and bottom but lost the middle — a finding called 'lost in the middle.' Why does long context cause this?
new.answer: Attention cost grows fast with length, and models train more on shorter texts, so middle positions get less focus.
choices: Attention cost grows fast with length, and models train more on shorter texts, so middle positions get less focus.
Bigger context windows force the model to forget its trained weights and require a fresh retraining run every week.
Bigger context windows are physically dangerous to operate above ten thousand tokens of input on any GPU in production.
Bigger context windows actively shrink the model's general knowledge to make room for the new input text in memory.
new.context: Liu et al. 'Lost in the Middle' (2023) showed retrieval performance is U-shaped: high near the start and end of the context, lower in the middle. Self-attention scales quadratically with sequence length, so long-context use is expensive in compute and slower at runtime. A 128K-token window does much more work than two 64K windows.
